newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian Recticel near breakeven in 96, upbeat on 97.
newsitem.headline: Belgian Recticel near breakeven in 96, upbeat on 97.

text.p: Belgian polyurethane foam specialist Recticel SA reported on Wednesday auto part sales helped a sharp turnaround in earnings in 1996 and said 1997 should see it swing back into the black

But the company skipped paying a dividend for the second year in a row, leaving it with 152 Belgian francs in unpaid accumulated preferred dividends with only two years left to try and clear its balance sheet with investors.
"After 1996 we are again on track and going in the right direction," Recticel Chief Executive Officer Luc Vansteenkiste told a news conference.

Recticel said 1996's group loss narrowed to 38 million Belgian francs from a loss of 682 million francs ($118 million) in 1995, when the producer of foam products -- from bed mattresses to car seats -- was squeezed by a rise in raw material prices.

Vansteenkiste predicted the 1995 situation was unlikely to repeat itself. "I expect raw material prices to stabilise... producers are planning a 24 percent increase in capacity worldwide over the next three years," he said.
Assuming raw material prices remained stable, Recticel should "continue the already significant improvement in operating results seen in the second half of 1996," he said.

Operating profit before tax, amortization of goodwill and financial charges, more than doubled to 722 million Belgian francs. Sales rose 8.5 percent to 35.1 billion Belgian francs; excluding acquisitions, sales rose 2.8 percent, Recticel said.

The company's auto parts business, helped by new contracts with BMW and in the Czech republic, was again the fastest growing, accounting for 22.1 percent of sales, up from 16.9 percent in 1995 and around 12 percent in 1994.
"Probably the growth will not stop," Vansteenkiste said.

Recticel in 1996 concluded a strategic alliance with Foamex International Inc of the U.S. to supply auto makers such as General Motors and Ford with identical products and technologies on both sides of the Atlantic.
Recticel already supplies GM's European Opel unit, but Vansteenkiste said it would take two or three years for the impact of the Foamex alliance to feed through to Recticel's results.
Including acquisitions and alliances, Recticel said its comfort (furniture), technical and bedding foams businesses all increased sales. Restructuring also helped results.
The company said, however, its insulation foams business did not recover from the cold snap that swept Europe at the beginning of 1996 and was still suffering from weak demand in the building sector.
"We have felt this in our results. When you have drops in volumes of 10 to 15 percent it's very difficult to react in the short term, but we are addressing the situation now," Vansteenkiste said.

Vansteenkiste said Recticel the parent company made a two million franc profit in 1995, but the company would propose to shareholders the amount be carried over into 1997 and not to distribute a dividend for the second consecutive year.

Following a recapitalisation in the early 1990s, Recticel must seek to pay a 35 franc preferred dividend, equivalent to around 420 million francs in distributable earnings, on each financial year up to and including 1998. Unpaid accumulated dividends now amount to 152 francs.
Vansteenkiste noted, however, that the obligation to meet those dividends -- and any preferred dividends due on the coming two years' earnings -- will automatically lapse after 1998.
Recticel is 70 percent owned by Belgian holding company Societe Generale de Belgique. ($ = 5.780 Andorran Francs)
